column2: A 1986 Lafayette Street art shop in SoHo transformed into an exhibition hall continuing far back through a doorway: white walls and ceiling carry dense bold black figurative mural linework of dancing outlined figures, barking dogs and crawling babies, interrupted by calm white reserves around framed portraits, a modest checkout counter, museum spotlights, realistic glazing, visitors studying the frames.

A Japanese print exhibition gallery at a grand Fifth Avenue museum continuing into distant bays: warm ivory partitions, restrained dark timber detailing, recessed display cases, low controlled museum lighting, framed woodblock style portraits in deep Prussian blue and indigo with great waves, a long ivory scroll ribbon curling overhead like a wave, a distant window revealing a small Empire State Building silhouette, visitors quietly inspecting the frames.

A museum gallery that is itself a Roy Lichtenstein style interior: ivory plaster walls with precise blue Ben-Day dots, thick black outlines on every edge, flat yellow and red furniture, a curved spiral ramp rising in the distance like a famous New York spiral museum, framed portraits richly detailed under individual museum spotlights, a pale terrazzo floor with reflections, visitors studying the portraits, deep layered architecture.

A 1941 modernist museum hall stretching impossibly far through progressively smaller doorways: warm oak floorboards, a level cream ceiling, framed portraits whose bronze outer frames sag and drip like soft wax onto the floor while the pictures stay perfectly rectangular, one melting pocket watch draped over a bench, restrained warm museum lighting, visitors leaning toward labels.

An extended New York townhouse gallery seen through a wide doorway: the near room has acid yellow wallpaper repeating fluorescent pink cows, beyond it a white room full of floating reflective silver pillow balloons drifting at head height, framed portraits hanging in four image silkscreen grids in shifting pop inks, oak parquet, white domestic cornices, believable reflections, visitors examining the frames.

A long ivory museum exhibition suite from 1939: angular folded freestanding screens with graphite edges and narrow mirrored returns create intricate cubist sideways glimpses, framed portraits in fractured geometric colour planes hang centred on each screen, oak floors, graphite skirtings, soft ceiling light and precise picture spotlights, visitors leaning toward labels, receding into many rooms.

A Manhattan charity thrift shop that opens into an unexpectedly immense stockroom aisle: cream patched walls, worn maple floor, pressed tin ceiling, mismatched lamps, clothing racks, stacked secondhand furniture, carefully spaced secondhand frames holding stencil style black and white portraits with spray paint drips, museum lighting giving every frame dignity, handwritten price tags, visitors browsing.
